drm_phases.prevention: BEFORE the event, avoiding new risk or reducing existing risk: risk assessment, land-use planning, building codes and enforcement, retrofitting, mitigation works, risk financing.
drm_phases.preparedness: BEFORE the event, capacities to anticipate, respond and recover: monitoring and early warning, contingency plans, drills, stockpiles, trained teams, public awareness, situational awareness systems.
drm_phases.response: DURING or IMMEDIATELY AFTER the event, saving lives and meeting basic needs: search and rescue, emergency health care, shelter, water, food, damage mapping, needs assessment, coordination, international assistance.
drm_phases.recovery: AFTER the event, restoring and improving livelihoods, services and assets (build back better): damage and loss assessment, reconstruction, rehabilitation, livelihoods and psychosocial support.

edge_status.planned: announced or planned, not yet done
edge_status.lacking: the documents say it was missing or failed

classes.definition: Physical event or process that can cause harm (main shock, aftershock, landslide, fire, outbreak).
Concrete effect on people, assets, services, economy or environment.
Pre-existing condition that increases susceptibility to earthquake impacts.
Action, plan, system, policy or capacity that reduces risk or impacts.
Unmet requirement or gap reported in the documents.
Organisation or group that acts.
People, property, systems or other elements present in hazard zones that are thereby subject to potential losses from an earthquake.
Vibratory motion of the ground produced by seismic waves radiating from an earthquake source; strength and duration depend on magnitude, distance to epicentre and local soil conditions.
Visible breaking and displacement of the earth's surface along the trace of a fault during an earthquake, including fissures and subsidence/uplift.
Smaller earthquake that follows a larger earthquake (mainshock) in the same area, caused by leftover stress along the fault line.
An earthquake that precedes a larger earthquake in the same sequence, often not recognized as such until the larger event occurs.
A separate earthquake of considerable magnitude caused by stress transfer from a main earthquake, which may occur outside the predicted aftershock area.
Mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope, including debris flow, triggered by earthquake shaking.
Process whereby water-saturated granular soil temporarily loses strength and behaves as a liquid due to earthquake shaking.
Series of ocean waves generated by sudden displacement of water, often triggered by submarine earthquakes.
Oscillation of water in an enclosed or semi-enclosed body of water, triggered by earthquake-induced ground motion.
Flooding caused as a secondary effect of an earthquake, e.g. due to dam or levee failure or changed river courses.
Uncontrolled combustion triggered as a secondary effect of an earthquake, often from damaged gas lines or electrical systems.
Accident triggered by an earthquake that damages hazardous installations, releasing hazardous substances leading to fires, explosions, gas leaks, or chemical spills.
Structural failure of a building during or after an earthquake, the leading cause of death and injury in earthquake disasters.
A person killed or injured as a direct result of an earthquake or its secondary hazards.
Population movement caused by destruction of homes or settling outside damaged buildings due to aftershock risk after an earthquake.
Quantifiable loss (economic, human, or physical) resulting from earthquake shaking and secondary hazards, calculated by combining hazard intensity, vulnerability functions and exposure data.
Damage to essential infrastructure such as power, telecommunications, water/sanitation, gas lines, ports, and airports, hampering relief efforts.
Susceptibility of buildings and infrastructure to damage from earthquake shaking, dependent on construction type, soil conditions and location.
Susceptibility of populations to earthquake impacts due to social, economic, or physical factors such as age, health, or belonging to a vulnerable group.
Structural intervention aimed at strengthening existing buildings to improve their resistance to earthquake shaking.
Design regulations with provisions for earthquake safety that buildings and civil engineering works must follow, enforced to mitigate earthquake risk.
Strategic land-use planning that forbids construction near cliff faces, active faults, or on soft soils to reduce earthquake risk.
System that detects earthquakes close to the source or fault rupture and sends real-time alerts to more distant locations, providing seconds to minutes of advance warning before shaking arrives.
Network of seismic stations/sensors used to observe and monitor seismic activity, essential for the effectiveness of early warning systems.
Automatic process (e.g., within GDACS) that estimates exposure, population, infrastructure impact and alert level for humanitarian activation shortly after an earthquake.
Specialized INSARAG-certified teams (USAR) tasked with detecting, locating and extracting survivors trapped in collapsed buildings and structures after an earthquake.
Inspection of earthquake-damaged infrastructure by certified structural engineers to determine safety for continued use.
Temporary housing solutions such as tents, cots, and blankets needed by people displaced by earthquake damage to homes.
Need for medical treatment, including temporary field hospitals with emergency medical personnel, supplies and equipment, to treat earthquake-injured individuals.
National or regional organization with the remit to monitor seismic activity and produce disaster risk data/information.
United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination team deployed to support coordination of international relief, including USAR operations, after an earthquake.

relations.definition: Source directly produces the target (a hazard, impact or vulnerability causes another hazard or impact).
A measure stops the target from happening at all (or would have, if recommended/lacking).
A measure reduces the severity or extent of the target.
A hazard sets off another (cascading) hazard, e.g. a main earthquake triggering an aftershock or secondary hazard.
A vulnerability or impact makes the target worse without causing it alone.
A measure responds to a need.
An actor carries out or provides a measure.
An aftershock or foreshock follows/precedes a mainshock earthquake in the same seismic sequence.
A seismic monitoring agency or network monitors earthquake activity to produce disaster risk data.
An early warning system or forecasting process warns of or estimates an earthquake's occurrence or impact.
The effectiveness of a measure depends on another measure (e.g., early warning system depending on the monitoring network).
A measure assesses the condition or safety of exposure elements (e.g. structural assessment of buildings).
A hazard or impact disrupts a measure or service (e.g., earthquake damage disrupting logistics).
Earthquake loss is calculated by combining seismic intensity/ground motion parameters with vulnerability functions and exposure datasets.
Vulnerability or exposure factors exacerbate the impacts of an earthquake.
An actor coordinates with another actor during earthquake response operations.

attributes.name: moment_magnitude
attributes.definition: Logarithmic measure of the total energy released by an earthquake, based on the seismic moment.

attributes.name: depth
attributes.definition: Depth below the earth's surface at which the earthquake rupture originates (focal depth); shallower earthquakes tend to cause more widespread surface damage.

attributes.name: seismic_intensity
attributes.definition: Qualitative measure of the severity of ground shaking at a location based on observed effects on humans, objects and nature (Modified Mercalli Intensity scale).

attributes.name: duration
attributes.definition: Length of time the earthquake shaking lasts, usually a minute or less.

attributes.name: epicentre_distance
attributes.definition: Distance from a given location to the earthquake's epicentre, influencing the strength of shaking felt there.

attributes.name: peak_ground_acceleration
attributes.definition: Ground motion parameter measuring the maximum acceleration experienced by the ground during an earthquake.

attributes.name: peak_ground_velocity
attributes.definition: Ground motion parameter measuring the maximum velocity of ground movement during an earthquake.

attributes.name: spectral_acceleration
attributes.definition: Elastic spectral acceleration for a given period of vibration, used to assess shaking intensity.

attributes.name: time_since_main_shock
attributes.definition: Elapsed time since the main earthquake, used to characterise temporal decay of aftershock frequency following Omori's law.

attributes.name: aftershock_frequency
attributes.definition: Rate of occurrence of aftershocks of a given magnitude following a main shock, decaying over time according to Omori's law.

attributes.name: number_of_deaths
attributes.definition: Count of people killed as a result of an earthquake and its associated secondary hazardous events.

attributes.name: number_of_injuries
attributes.definition: Count of injured persons resulting from an earthquake disaster.

attributes.name: survival_time
attributes.definition: Length of time a victim trapped under rubble can survive, with 85-95% rescued alive within 24-48 hours.

attributes.name: population_count
attributes.definition: Number of people exposed to an earthquake hazard, estimated as part of rapid impact estimation.

attributes.name: structural_resilience
attributes.definition: Degree to which a building can withstand seismic shaking without collapsing, influenced by design, construction quality, and compliance with seismic codes.

attributes.name: lead_time
attributes.definition: Amount of advance warning time (seconds to minutes) provided by an early warning system before the arrival of strong shaking.
